usage: Just like English, 죽다 covers batteries and phones going dead — 배터리/핸드폰이 죽다.
I could die, it's so hard
An adjective + 죽겠어요 is everyday exaggeration ('so X I could die'), never literal.
For people you respect, switch 죽다 to the honorific 돌아가시다 — saying 죽었어요 about an elder is rude.
죽을 뻔하다 = 'nearly died/almost', a fixed pattern for a close call.
examples: 꽃이 다 죽었어요
The flowers all died
Plants and animals dying take 죽다 directly; the subject takes 이/가.
배고파 죽겠어요
I'm starving to death
The most common spoken use: feeling + 죽겠어요 to dramatize, said casually among friends.
오래된 핸드폰이 또 죽었어요
My old phone died again
Machines/devices losing power 'die' in Korean exactly as in English.
nuance: 죽다 is the plain, blunt word for 'to die', and that bluntness matters: Koreans almost never say it literally about a person they respect — there you use the honorific 돌아가시다 (literally 'to return/go back'), so 할아버지가 돌아가셨어요, never 죽었어요. By far the most frequent everyday use is the exaggeration '-아/어 죽겠어요' bolted onto a feeling: 배고파 죽겠어요, 더워 죽겠어요, 심심해 죽겠어요 ('so bored I could die'). It also works literally for plants, animals, and dead machines/batteries (핸드폰이 죽었어요). The big English-speaker pitfall is the causative: 죽다 is intransitive ('die'), so to say someone *kills* you add 이 → 죽이다 ('to kill'); 모기를 죽이다 = 'kill a mosquito', and 죽다 can never take a 을/를 object. As a regular consonant-stem verb it just adds 어요: 죽 + 어요 → 죽어요.

usage: 놀다 means 'spend fun time / hang out', not just children's play; the partner takes 하고/랑.
If you're free today, let's hang out
Casual 놀자 is how friends invite each other to meet up.
Let's go out / go have fun
놀러 가다 = 'go somewhere to enjoy yourself', a super-common invitation frame.
놀다 also covers doing nothing productive — relaxing, not literally playing.
examples: 주말에 친구하고 놀아요
I hang out with friends on the weekend
The default way to describe weekend plans with people.
아이들이 공원에서 놀아요
The kids are playing in the park
Children physically playing uses the very same verb; the place takes 에서.
우리 집에서 놀까요?
Shall we hang out at my place?
놀까요? proposes meeting up to relax together, warm and casual.
nuance: 놀다 spans a wide range English splits into different words: children 'playing', adults 'hanging out', and even 'goofing off / doing nothing productive' (그냥 집에서 놀았어요 = 'I just chilled at home'). That makes it one of the most-used social verbs, and the friendly invitation 놀자 / 같이 놀래? is core friend vocabulary. Watch the register: 놀다 carries a relaxed, fun, sometimes idle feeling, so you would not use it for a serious meeting — for that you'd say 만나다 ('meet'). It's a ㄹ-irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ, which is why you get 놉니다 (not 놀습니다) and the honorific command 노세요 (not 놀세요/놀으세요), while the plain 어요-form keeps the ㄹ → 놀 + 아요 → 놀아요. The English-speaker trap is forcing 'play an instrument/sport' onto 놀다 — those use different verbs (피아노를 치다, 축구를 하다), and 놀다 is the social/leisure sense only.

usage: 걸리다 with 시간 is THE way to ask about duration; the time, not you, is the subject.
감기에 걸리다 = 'catch a cold'; the illness takes 에, not 를.
걸리다 also means 'be caught/busted' — getting caught by a person or rule.
A painting is hanging on the wall
걸리다 is the passive of 걸다 ('to hang'), so things hang/are caught on something.
examples: 집까지 한 시간 걸려요
It takes an hour to get home
Travel time: the duration is the subject — 한 시간이 걸려요.
또 감기에 걸렸어요
I caught a cold again
A fixed expression every beginner needs; note the 에 particle.
과속하다가 경찰한테 걸렸어요
I was speeding and got caught by the police
The 'get busted' sense, with the catcher marked by 한테.
nuance: 걸리다 is a high-frequency verb that fans out into three everyday senses learners meet fast: (1) time being needed — 시간이 걸리다; (2) catching an illness — 감기에 걸리다; and (3) getting caught/busted — 경찰한테 걸리다, 거짓말이 걸리다. The thread linking them is its origin as the passive of 걸다 ('to hang/hook'): something gets hooked — by time, by sickness, by the law — so 벽에 그림이 걸려 있어요 ('a picture is hung on the wall') is the same word. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the subject/particle: for 'take time' the *time* is the subject (시간이 걸려요), never 시간을 걸려요; and for illness you must use 에 (감기에 걸리다), not the object 를. Compare 걸리다 ('take/require time') with 들다, which is used for cost/effort/money (돈이 들다) — 시간이 걸리다 vs 돈이 들다 is a pairing Koreans keep distinct. It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 걸리 + 어 contracts to 걸려요.

usage: Physical crossing of a height (mountain, wall, hill) takes 을/를.
넘다 also means a time/number has been exceeded; the figure takes 이/가.
넘다 carries the figurative 'overstep a boundary' sense too, just like English.
넘게 = 'more than/over', a handy adverbial form for amounts.
examples: 저 산을 천천히 넘어요
I slowly go over that mountain
Physically going over a height; what you cross is the 을/를 object.
벌써 열두 시가 넘었어요
It's already past midnight
A point in time being passed — the time takes 이/가.
참가자가 백 명이 넘어요
There are over a hundred participants
Used for a count exceeding a number.
nuance: 넘다 means to go over or pass beyond a limit — a wall, a mountain pass, a number, a clock time, or even a social boundary (선을 넘다 = 'cross the line', exactly like the English idiom). The crucial English-speaker pitfall is that the particle flips with the meaning: for physically crossing something the object takes 을/를 (산을 넘다), but for *exceeding* a number or time the figure becomes the subject with 이/가 (열 시가 넘었어요, 만 원이 넘어요), not 을/를. Keep 넘다 ('cross/exceed') apart from 건너다, which is for crossing a flat span like a street or river (길을 건너다) — 넘다 implies getting over a height or threshold, 건너다 implies going across to the other side. It is a regular consonant-stem verb: 넘 + 어요 → 넘어요. Do not confuse it with the excluded 넘어지다 ('to fall over/trip'), which looks related but describes losing your balance.

Don't mix up 넘다 (go over a height/limit) with 건너다 (cross a street/river) — 길은 건너고, 산은 넘습니다.

usage: 놓치다 = fail to catch a bus/train/flight; the thing missed takes 을/를.
기회를 놓치다 is a very common warning/advice collocation.
놓치다 covers failing to grasp/notice something — a point, a detail, a chance.
놓칠 뻔하다 = 'nearly missed it', a near-miss with transport.
examples: 방금 버스를 놓쳤어요
I just missed the bus
The most typical use, for transport you failed to catch.
지하철을 놓쳐서 늦었어요
I was late because I missed the subway
Pairs naturally with 늦다 in everyday excuses (-아서 gives the reason).
이런 좋은 기회를 놓치면 안 돼요
You shouldn't miss a good chance like this
Opportunities use 놓치다 too; -면 안 되다 gives the 'mustn't' warning.
nuance: 놓치다 is for missing something you were actively trying to catch or hold — a bus, a train, a flight, a chance, or even the thread of a conversation (요점을 놓치다 = 'miss the point') — and it always takes a 을/를 object. Its make-up shows the meaning: 놓다 ('to let go/release') + 치다, so it literally pictures something slipping out of your grasp. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is using it for missing a *person*: English 'I miss you' is NOT 놓치다 — that is 보고 싶다 ('want to see'), so 엄마가 보고 싶어요, never 엄마를 놓쳐요. Contrast 놓치다 ('fail to catch what was within reach') with 지나가다/지나치다 ('let pass / pass by'): you 놓치다 a bus you ran for, but a chance that quietly 지나가다 simply went by. It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 놓치 + 어 → 놓쳐요, and it frequently appears alongside 늦다 ('be late').

Don't drop the object marker: it's 버스를 놓쳤어요, since 놓치다 is transitive and needs a 을/를 object.

usage: 떨어지다 also means a supply is used up; what runs out takes 이/가.
The cup fell on the floor
Basic 'fall down' meaning; the landing place takes 에.
시험/면접에 떨어지다 = fail a test/interview, the opposite of 붙다.
떨어지다 idiomatically means a cold/illness 'going away' — 감기가 떨어지다.
examples: 휴지가 다 떨어졌어요
We're all out of tissues
Daily use for supplies running out; pair with 다 ('all').
지갑이 바닥에 떨어졌어요
My wallet fell on the floor
Something dropping by itself to the ground — intransitive.
이번에도 시험에 떨어졌어요
I failed the exam this time too
Failing a test takes 에; its positive partner is 붙다 ('pass').
nuance: 떨어지다 is the intransitive 'fall' — something drops on its own (지갑이 떨어졌어요), with no doer — and it branches into two more senses beginners hit immediately: a supply running out (돈이/휴지가 떨어졌어요) and failing an exam or interview (시험에 떨어졌어요, the opposite of 붙다 'to pass'). The form already signals intransitivity: it's built on the 지다 pattern ('come to be / get'), so 떨어지 + 어 → 떨어져요. The headline English-speaker pitfall is transitivity: 떨어지다 can never take a 을/를 object, so to say *you* drop something you must switch to the transitive 떨어뜨리다 — 컵을 떨어뜨렸어요 ('I dropped the cup') vs 컵이 떨어졌어요 ('the cup fell'). Also distinguish 떨어지다 ('drop/fall, used up') from 넘어지다 ('topple over, lose balance'): a wallet 떨어지다 to the floor, but a person 넘어지다.

For failing a test use 에: 시험에 떨어졌어요, not 시험을 떨어졌어요; its positive counterpart is 시험에 붙다.

usage: 오르다 is the go-to verb for prices/numbers rising; what rises takes 이/가.
오르다 can mean climbing up; the destination takes 에, not 을.
월급/연봉이 오르다 = get a raise, a natural everyday collocation.
Abstract levels — 인기, 실력, 기온 — also 오르다.
examples: 요즘 물가가 많이 올랐어요
The cost of living has risen a lot lately
Very common with 물가; the past 올랐어요 shows the 르-irregular.
기온이 갑자기 올랐어요
The temperature suddenly rose
Used for temperature climbing; 이/가 marks what rises.
우리 같이 산에 올라요
Let's climb the mountain together
Climbing upward — the place you ascend to takes 에.
nuance: 오르다 means to rise or go up — prices, temperature, a salary, popularity, or your body climbing a mountain (산에 오르다). For the everyday 'prices are up' complaint Koreans reach for 값이 올랐어요 / 물가가 올랐어요, and for a raise, 월급이 올랐어요. The conjugation is the classic 르-irregular and the headline pitfall for learners: before -아/어 the 르 drops its ㅡ and an extra ㄹ is inserted onto the previous syllable, so 오르 + 아 → 올라요 and the past is 올랐어요, never the naive 오르어요/오르었어요. Two boundaries to keep clear: (1) 오르다 ('go up, rise') is intransitive — to *raise* a price yourself you use the transitive 올리다 (가격을 올리다); and (2) compare 오르다 ('climb up onto/ascend', often goal-focused: 정상에 오르다 'reach the summit') with the excluded directional 올라가다 ('go up' as movement away from you).

오르다 is intransitive ('rise'); to *raise* something yourself use the transitive 올리다 — 가격을 올리다, not 가격을 오르다.

usage: Used when water/things won't come out of a tap; the source takes 에서.
What time do you head out (leave)?
나오다 also means coming out of / leaving a place toward the speaker.
음식이 나오다 = food being served/brought out, restaurant staple.
나오다 means 'appear/feature' in media — TV에/뉴스에 나오다.
examples: 주문한 음식이 다 나왔어요
All the food I ordered has come out
Said when dishes are served at a restaurant.
수도에서 물이 안 나와요
Water isn't coming out of the tap
A common household complaint; 에서 marks where it comes from.
회사에서 보통 몇 시에 나와요?
What time do you usually get off work?
Leaving a workplace, moving out toward the listener.
nuance: 나오다 is 'come out' — emerging toward the speaker or out of an enclosed place — and it's built transparently from 나 ('out') + 오다 ('come'). Because Korean bakes direction into the verb, it pairs with 나가다 ('go out', away from the speaker): the very same English 'come/go out' splits depending on where you stand, so a waiter bringing food says 음식이 나와요, but you stepping outside say 밖에 나가요. Beyond the literal, it's everywhere for water/gas running (물이 안 나와요), food being served (음식이 나왔어요), people leaving work (회사에서 나오다), and appearing in media (TV에 나오다). The conjugation pitfall: the stem ends in 오, and 오 + 아 contracts to 와, giving 나와요 and past 나왔어요 (not 나오아요). The directional pitfall is the big one — don't default to 나오다 for every 'go out'; if the motion is away from you, it must be 나가다.

usage: 넣다 = put a thing into a place; the thing takes 을/를.
I put the book in the bag
The destination/container takes 에 — 가방에 넣다.
넣다 also means 'enter/fill in' a form field.
I put money into my account
돈을 통장에 넣다 = deposit money; a natural finance collocation.
examples: 커피에 설탕을 넣어요
I put sugar in the coffee
Everyday food/drink use; 에 marks what you put it into.
가방에 지갑을 넣었어요
I put my wallet in the bag
Putting an object inside something — thing + 을/를, place + 에.
신청서에 이름을 넣으세요
Please put your name on the application
The 'fill in / enter' sense, common with forms.
nuance: 넣다 means to put or insert something into a place or container, so it is a two-slot verb: it needs both the thing (을/를) and the destination (에) — 가방에 책을 넣어요. From that core it stretches to filling in forms (이름을 넣다), depositing money (통장에 돈을 넣다), and adding ingredients while cooking. The pronunciation/spelling pitfall for English speakers is the stem-final ㅎ: unlike ㅎ-irregular *adjectives* (빨갛다 → 빨개요), verbs ending in ㅎ are perfectly regular and keep the ㅎ in writing, so it's 넣 + 어요 → 넣어요 and past 넣었어요 (never 너어요 / 너었어요), even though the ㅎ is barely heard. Mind the particle, too: the destination is 에 (the static location 'into'), not 에서 (which marks a source) — that 에 vs 에서 split is exactly what separates 넣다 ('put into', 에) from its opposite 빼다 ('take out from', 에서).

usage: 빼다 + 주세요 is how you ask for an ingredient to be removed when ordering.
I took the book out of the bag
The source takes 에서 — the opposite particle to 넣다's 에.
빼다 is the math 'subtract'; you subtract 을/를 from 에서.
살을 빼다 = lose weight, an extremely common idiomatic collocation.
examples: 김밥에서 오이를 빼 주세요
Please take the cucumber out of the gimbap
Super useful when ordering food; 에서 marks where it's removed from.
주머니에서 손을 뺐어요
I took my hand out of my pocket
Removing something from a place — note the contracted past 뺐어요.
요즘 살을 빼려고 운동해요
I'm exercising to lose weight these days
The idiom 살을 빼다 ('lose weight') with -려고 ('in order to').
nuance: 빼다 means to take something out, remove it, leave it off, or — in math — subtract, and it's the natural transitive opposite of 넣다 ('put in'). The particle pitfall mirrors 넣다 exactly: the source takes 에서 ('out from'), so 가방에서 빼다, not 가방에 빼다. The conjugation pitfall is the contraction: the stem ends in ㅐ, and ㅐ + 어 simply merges, so the present is 빼요 (not 빼어요) and the past is 뺐어요 (not 빼었어요). Distinguish 빼다 ('remove/extract, transitive') from the intransitive 빠지다 ('fall out / drop out / be excluded'): you 빼다 a name from a list, but a name 빠지다 (goes missing) from it.

usage: 차다 = kick, most often with 공 (a ball); what you kick takes 을/를.
I kick the ball with my foot
발로 = 'with the foot'; the instrument takes 로/으로.
I got dumped by my boyfriend
차이다 (passive of 차다) = get dumped — a hugely common slang use.
Same sound 차다 also means 'wear' a watch/bracelet — context tells them apart.
examples: 공을 세게 차요
I kick the ball hard
Most common with 공; 세게 ('hard') is a natural adverb partner.
아이가 돌을 찼어요
The child kicked a stone
Simple past; note the contracted 찼어요 from the ㅏ stem.
우리 같이 축구공 찰까요?
Shall we go kick a soccer ball?
An invitation to play; 찰까요? proposes doing it together.
nuance: 차다 most commonly means to kick, taking a 을/를 object for what's kicked (공을 차다), and the instrument 'with the foot' takes 로 → 발로 차다. It conjugates as a regular ㅏ-stem verb where ㅏ + 아 contracts: 차 + 아 → 차요, past 찼어요 (not 차아요). The thing to flag for learners is that 차다 is really three homophones sharing a spelling: (1) 'kick'; (2) 'be full / fill up' (방이 사람으로 가득 찼어요 'the room filled with people'); and (3) 'wear' a watch or bracelet (시계를 차다) — context disambiguates, and as a beginner you should lock in 'kick' first. There's also a high-frequency slang spin via the passive 차이다: 차다 someone = 'dump' a partner, and 차이다 = 'get dumped' (남자친구한테 차였어요), which surprises English speakers. Don't confuse 차다 ('kick') with 치다, the verb for hitting/striking (테니스를 치다, 박수를 치다) — feet 차다, hands/rackets 치다.

Don't use 차다 for hitting with the hand or a racket — that's 치다 (박수를 치다, 테니스를 치다); 차다 is kicking with the foot.

usage: 밟다 = tread on something; what you step on takes 을/를.
Be careful, don't step on it
밟지 마세요 is a frequent warning not to tread on something.
Stepping on something unpleasant on the ground.
액셀/브레이크를 밟다 = press the accelerator/brake, a driving collocation.
examples: 미안해요, 발을 밟았어요
Sorry, I stepped on your foot
Said after bumping someone in a crowd; pairs with 미안해요/죄송해요.
길에서 껌을 밟았어요
I stepped on gum on the street
Treading on something on the ground; the place takes 에서.
꽃을 밟지 마세요
Please don't step on the flowers
A polite request not to tread on something.
nuance: 밟다 means to step on or tread on something, taking a 을/를 object, and in daily life it shows up constantly in two settings: apologizing after stepping on someone in a crowd (발을 밟았어요 + 죄송해요) and driving, where you 밟다 the pedals — 액셀을 밟다 ('hit the gas'), 브레이크를 밟다 ('hit the brakes'). The conjugation is the classic trap: the spelling has the double final ㄼ and *looks* like it might be ㅂ-irregular, but 밟다 is fully regular — the ㅂ stays, so it's 밟 + 아요 → 밟아요 and past 밟았어요, never anything like 발워요. (Pronunciation note: the standard reading keeps the ㅂ, roughly 'bal-ba-yo'.) For meaning, keep 밟다 ('step on, with downward foot pressure') apart from 차다 ('kick', a striking motion) and from 디디다 ('plant/set your foot down', as in taking a step or gaining a foothold) — 밟다 emphasizes pressing down onto whatever is underfoot.

usage: 다니다 = regularly go to a place like school/work; the place takes 에.
회사에 다니다 is the standard way to say where you work.
I've been going to the hospital (for treatment)
다니다 implies repeated visits over time, not one trip.
다니다 also means 'go about / move around', as in everyday going-and-coming.
examples: 저는 한국어 학원에 다녀요
I attend a Korean language academy
Regular attendance at a school/academy; the institution takes 에.
큰 회사에 다녀요
I work at a big company
다니다 = 'attend/commute to' a workplace, the natural 'I work at' verb.
요즘 헬스장에 다녀요
I've been going to the gym these days
Habitually attending a place over a stretch of time.
nuance: 다니다 means to go to a place habitually — attend school, commute to a job, frequent the gym, keep going to a clinic — so it always implies repetition and an ongoing relationship, not a single trip; it also covers plain 'go about / get around' (밤에 혼자 다니지 마 'don't go around alone at night'). The place attended takes 에 (학교에 다녀요), and it's a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 다니 + 어 → 다녀요. The key English-speaker pitfall is choosing the wrong 'go' verb: to state where you study or work, 다니다 is right because it conveys 'regularly attend' — 회사에 다녀요 ('I work at a company') — whereas 회사에 가요 would mean a single 'I'm going to the office (right now)'. Contrast 다니다 (habitual, ongoing attendance) with 가다 (one directional trip) and 출근하다 (the specific act of 'going in to work' on a given day): you 다니다 a company in general but 출근하다 each morning.

english: to stop (a vehicle) / to stand up
usage: 세워 주세요 is the essential phrase for getting out of a taxi.
I stopped / pulled over the car
세우다 = bring a vehicle to a stop; the car takes 을/를.
세우다 also means standing an object up vertically.
계획을 세우다 = make/set up a plan, a very common abstract collocation.
examples: 기사님, 여기 세워 주세요
Driver, please stop here
The key taxi sentence for getting out; 기사님 addresses the driver politely.
저 앞에서 세워 주세요
Please stop just up ahead
Pointing out where to pull over; 에서 marks the spot.
여행 계획을 세웠어요
I made a travel plan
The abstract sense 'set up a plan', built on the same 'make stand' image.
nuance: 세우다 is the transitive 'make (something) stand / bring to a stop', and it's the causative partner of 서다 ('to stand still / come to a stop, by itself'): 서다 is what a car does on its own, 세우다 is you stopping it. The must-memorize phrase is 여기 세워 주세요 ('please stop here'), the standard way to get a taxi to pull over. Its 'make stand' core also yields the very common abstract 계획을 세우다 ('make a plan', literally 'set a plan upright'). Conjugation pitfall: the stem ends in 우, and 우 + 어 contracts to 워, so the present is 세워요 and the past 세웠어요 (not 세우어요). The transitivity pitfall is the one to drill: 세우다 takes a 을/를 object (차를 세우다 = 'stop the car'), while the intransitive 서다 doesn't (차가 섰어요 = 'the car stopped') — English uses 'stop' for both, so learners wrongly say 차가 세워요. Tell a driver to stop with 세우다; describe a car halting by itself with 서다.
